total:
\(\text{Adaptivity is worth an exponential in the noisy model too}\) total Gap #

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}(\mathrm{ADDR}_k) = O(k) \text{ while } \mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(\mathrm{ADDR}_k) = \Theta(2^k)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{ADDR}_k\) BenDavidBlais20composition

Same reason as in the query model: a non-adaptive schedule has to spread its bias budget over the whole table, while an adaptive one reads the address first and then spends everything on the one cell it needs. The non-adaptive value is Theorem 8 of [BenDavidBlais20composition] applied to $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(\mathrm{ADDR}_k)=\Theta(2^k)$.

So the two ways of weakening $\mathrm{R}$ -- charge less for less information, or forbid looking at the answers -- are not comparable, and combining them changes nothing: $\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}} = \Theta(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}})$.

see also: \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{ADDR}_k\), \(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\) data/relations/04-composition.yaml

facts: Theorem 8 of [BenDavidBlais20composition]: $\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) = \Theta(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f))$ for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$. Non-adaptively, buying cheap bias buys nothing at all.

This is false for relations: on the \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\) family of [GLSS19], $\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}} = O(1)$ while $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}} = \Omega(\sqrt n)$. The proof of Theorem 8 therefore has to "notice" that $f$ is a function, which is unusual in query complexity.
The adaptive analogue is exactly Is …?, and is false as an exact $\Theta$ for partial $f$ (\(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\)).

The proof goes through Samorodnitsky's inequality [Samorodnitsky16, PolyanskiyWu17]: a noisy copy at bias $\rho$ tells you at least as much about $f(X)$ as an erasure copy that survives with probability $\rho^2$. Erasures are honest queries, so the noisy budget can be converted into a query budget -- and it is the entropy-to-error step (Fano / [HellmanRaviv70]) that breaks for relations.
self.name: Non-adaptive noisy randomized query complexity
self.short: The bias-purchasing model with the whole schedule of biases committed to in advance.

partial:
\(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) = \Theta\big(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\big)\) partial Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) \le \mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Immediate: a real query is a noisy query at bias $1$, and the budget $\sum_i\gamma_i^2$ then counts queries.
  • \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) = O\big(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\big)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition Samorodnitsky16 PolyanskiyWu17
    Theorem 8, for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$: non-adaptively, buying cheap bias buys nothing. The route is an information-theoretic exchange rate. Samorodnitsky's inequality [Samorodnitsky16], in the form isolated by [PolyanskiyWu17], says that a noisy copy of $X$ at bias $\rho$ carries at least as much information about $f(X)$ as an erasure copy that survives with probability $\rho^2$ -- and $\rho^2$ is exactly what the noisy model charges. Erasures are honest queries, so a noisy algorithm of cost $c$ converts into a distribution over query sets of expected size $O(c)$ that leaves as little entropy in $f(X)$; a non-adaptive minimax lemma turns the distributional statement back into a worst-case algorithm, and Fano / [HellmanRaviv70] turns the entropy bound into an error bound.

The non-adaptive shadow of Is …?, and the only case of it that is settled. Adaptively the analogous statement is false for partial functions -- $\mathrm{R}$ can be exponentially larger than $\mathrm{noisyR}$ on \(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\) -- so adaptivity is what lets an algorithm spend a statistical budget the query model cannot match.

The theorem is also false for relations (\(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\)), which is unusual: almost every argument in query complexity is indifferent to whether the output is Boolean. The step that notices is the last one, from entropy to error probability.

see also: \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\), \(\mathrm{ApproxIndex}_k\), Is …? data/relations/04-composition.yaml

relation Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f) \le \mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\)
    BenDavidBlais20composition
    Setting every $\gamma_i \in \{0,1\}$ turns a noisy non-adaptive algorithm into an ordinary one and back; the cost $\sum_i \gamma_i^2$ becomes $|S|$.

The easy half of Theorem 8. The hard half -- $\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}} = O(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}})$ -- holds for partial Boolean functions and is false for relations, so it is recorded one setting down.

see also: \(\mathrm{noisyR}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{AGREE}_n\) data/relations/13-definitional.yaml
